notes: Brief gives no starting leader: ruling slot 1 holds the UDR of President Pompidou and Prime Minister Chaban-Delmas (name Union des démocrates pour la République since October 1968, secretary-general Robert Poujade). The coalition slot 2 is the real junior partner, Giscard's FNRI; the Duhamel centrists (CDP) are mentioned in the Centre démocrate text. Centre démocrate (Lecanuet/Poher) placed in slot 14 for its starting popularity. Slot 6 holds the orthodox Gaullists (anti-Atlanticist, pro-détente), slot 13 the ENA technocracy, slot 0 the SAC. Ligue communiste (Krivine) takes slot 5 instead of MD's LO; Gauche prolétarienne in 19 (Maoist) instead of MD's Fédération anarchiste. Slot 20 switches from Nicoud's CID shopkeepers' revolt to the Front national on 5 Oct 1972. UDR and FNRI sprites not reused (RPR/UDF logos); PS, PCF, armed forces and Bourbon(-Orléans) sprites reused.

0.name: Service d'action civique
0.text:
The Civic Action Service is the Gaullist movement's own security force, founded in 1960 from the stewards of the old Rally of the French People. Its patron is Jacques Foccart, the Élysée's secretary-general for African affairs, and it is run by Pierre Debizet. In May 1968 it helped organise the great Gaullist march on the Champs-Élysées and the Committees for the Defence of the Republic.

The SAC sees itself as the shield of the Fifth Republic against communist subversion and leftist street violence. It provides bodyguards, poster squads and informers, recruits among policemen, veterans and the underworld, and works with friendly intelligence services in France and Africa. Its methods are those of a parallel police, and its leverage lies in intimidation, secrets and the protection of powerful patrons.

1.name: Union des démocrates pour la République
1.english: Union of Democrats for the Republic
1.native_full: Union des démocrates pour la République
1.text:
The Union of Democrats for the Republic is the Gaullist party, heir to the Union for the New Republic created in 1958 to support General de Gaulle. Since the landslide of June 1968 it holds an absolute majority in the Assembly on its own. Since de Gaulle's resignation in April 1969 it has served President Georges Pompidou, while Prime Minister Jacques Chaban-Delmas promises a 'New Society' and Robert Poujade runs the party as secretary-general.

The UDR stands for a strong presidency, national independence, the nuclear strike force, détente with Moscow and a Europe of nations. It defends order and economic modernisation while debating how far to liberalise. Its voters span the Catholic provinces, the middle classes and part of the working class, and it holds every lever of the state.
1.wiki: Union of Democrats for the Republic

2.name: Fédération nationale des républicains indépendants
2.text:
The National Federation of Independent Republicans was founded in 1966 by Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, who in 1962 had led the pro-Gaullist wing of the National Centre of Independents and Peasants into the majority. Its 'yes, but' to Gaullism became open defiance when Giscard opposed the referendum of April 1969, yet under Pompidou he has returned as Minister of Economy and Finance, while his ally Raymond Marcellin runs the Interior Ministry.

The Independent Republicans are the junior partner of the majority: liberal, pro-European and more Atlanticist than the Gaullists. They champion free enterprise, sound money, modern management and a centrist, technocratic style. Their base lies among provincial notables, business leaders and the Catholic bourgeoisie, and their leverage is Giscard's ambition to inherit the presidency.

3.name: Parti socialiste
3.text:
The Socialist Party was founded in 1969, at the congresses of Alfortville and Issy-les-Moulineaux, when the old French Section of the Workers' International merged with the socialist clubs of Alain Savary and Jean Poperen. Savary is first secretary, but Guy Mollet's apparatus still holds many federations, and the party is reeling from Gaston Defferre's humiliating five per cent in the 1969 presidential election. François Mitterrand's Convention of Republican Institutions remains outside.

The party seeks a democratic road to socialism through planning, nationalisations and social reform, and is debating a union of the left with the Communists. It supports European integration and the Atlantic Alliance. Its strength lies among teachers and civil servants, in the municipal machines of the Nord, Pas-de-Calais and Marseille, and in the Force ouvrière unions.

4.name: Parti communiste français
4.text:
The French Communist Party, founded at the Congress of Tours in 1920, is the largest party of the French left: Jacques Duclos won 21 per cent in the 1969 presidential election. Its secretary-general Waldeck Rochet is in failing health, Georges Marchais is rising through the apparatus, and the philosopher Roger Garaudy openly challenges the leadership after the party's criticism of the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The PCF seeks an 'advanced democracy' opening the road to socialism through a common programme with the Socialists. It remains loyal to the Soviet Union and opposes NATO and the Europe of monopolies. Its power rests on the CGT trade union confederation, the red belt of municipalities around Paris, the industrial north and its daily L'Humanité.

5.name: Ligue communiste
5.text:
The Communist League was founded in April 1969 as the French section of the Fourth International by militants of the Revolutionary Communist Youth, which the government dissolved after May 1968. Its best-known figure, Alain Krivine, ran for president in 1969 while doing military service and won just over one per cent; Daniel Bensaïd and Henri Weber are among its leading intellectuals, and its paper is Rouge.

The League preaches world revolution, workers' councils and the overthrow of capitalism, and condemns both Gaullism and the Stalinist bureaucracies of the East. It mobilises for Vietnam and against repression, and dreams of a new May 1968 that would reach the factories. Its base lies among students, lycée pupils and young teachers, and its leverage in the energy it can bring to the streets.

6.name: Les Gardiens du temple
6.text:
The Guardians of the Temple are the orthodox Gaullists who fear that Georges Pompidou is diluting the General's legacy. Their figurehead is Michel Debré, Minister of National Defence and father of the 1958 constitution, and they watch every step of Chaban-Delmas's opening to the centrists with suspicion, while de Gaulle himself keeps silent at Colombey, writing his memoirs.

They defend total national independence: the nuclear strike force, withdrawal from NATO's integrated command, a Europe of nations without supranational institutions and wariness of British entry. They favour détente with Moscow, friendship with the Arab world and distance from Washington. Their base lies in the old Resistance and Free French networks, and their leverage in their moral authority and their weight in the UDR group.

7.name: Les Thoréziens
7.text:
The Thorezians are the Stalinist old guard of the French Communist Party, loyal to the memory of Maurice Thorez, who led the party from 1930 until his death in 1964. Their emblem is his widow Jeannette Vermeersch, who left the Political Bureau in October 1968 rather than accept the party's disapproval of the Warsaw Pact intervention in Czechoslovakia.

They hold that the Soviet Union is the leader of the world communist movement and that criticism of Moscow only serves imperialism. They distrust the opening to the Socialists, despise Garaudy's revisionism and the student leftists, and prize discipline over debate. Their base is older militants from the Resistance and Cold War years, and their leverage lies in ties to the Soviet embassy and to Moscow-trained cadres.

8.name: Nehzat-e Azadi-ye Iran
8.text:
The Freedom Movement of Iran was founded in 1961 by the engineer Mehdi Bazargan, Ayatollah Mahmoud Taleghani and Yadollah Sahabi as the religious wing of Mosaddegh's nationalist camp. Its founders received long prison terms after the uprising of 1963, and the movement is kept alive largely by Iranian students and exiles abroad, including a circle in Paris that circulates its tracts among the city's Iranian community.

The movement blends Shia faith with constitutionalism, social justice and national independence. It wants the Shah to reign rather than rule, free elections, an end to SAVAK repression and freedom from American and British tutelage, and it rejects both Marxism and clerical rule. Its leverage lies in the respect of the educated middle class, the bazaar and reformist clergy.

9.name: Hey'at-ha-ye Mo'talefeh-ye Eslami
9.text:
The Islamic Coalition, or Mo'talefeh, was formed in 1963 when religious societies of the Tehran bazaar united behind Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, now exiled in Najaf. In January 1965 its gunmen assassinated Prime Minister Hassan Ali Mansur; several members were executed and the rest went underground. Devout Iranian students and merchants travelling to Paris discreetly carry Khomeini's sermons and the Coalition's appeals to the faithful abroad.

The Coalition wants the Shah overthrown and an Islamic order guided by the senior clergy, with Khomeini as its leader. It denounces the Pahlavi dynasty's ties to America and Israel and the secular reforms of the White Revolution. Its strength lies in bazaar money, mosque networks and religious dues, and its leverage in its capacity for disciplined clandestine action.

10.name: Grande Mosquée de Paris
10.text:
The Grand Mosque of Paris was built between 1922 and 1926 as the Republic's tribute to the Muslim soldiers who died for France in the Great War. Its rector since 1957, Si Hamza Boubakeur, a former deputy for the Sahara in the National Assembly, has kept it under French influence, to the anger of the Algerian government, which claims the right to run it.

The mosque represents an official, conservative Sunni Islam: prayers, religious holidays, marriages, burials and representation before the authorities. It preaches loyalty to France and keeps away from the politics of North Africa and the Middle East. Its audience is the older generation of Algerian workers, harkis and Muslim notables, and its leverage lies in the backing of the French state and of conservative Arab monarchies.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani and is outlawed across the Arab world for its attempts to infiltrate the armed forces. In Paris, a few Syrian, Jordanian, Palestinian and Tunisian students keep discreet study circles, wary of both the French police and the informers of their own embassies.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy, socialism and every existing Muslim regime, and calls for a single caliphate governing by Islamic law that would unite the Muslims and liberate Palestine. For now it shuns violence, preferring propaganda and the winning over of officers and elites. In France it has no organisation of weight; its influence is limited to the student hostels of the Latin Quarter and the Cité universitaire.

12.name: Association des étudiants islamiques en France
12.english: Association of Islamic Students in France
12.native_full: Association des étudiants islamiques en France
12.text:
The Association of Islamic Students in France was founded in 1963 by Muhammad Hamidullah, the Hyderabad-born scholar of the National Centre for Scientific Research whose French translation of the Quran is widely read. It brings together Arab, Turkish, African and South Asian students in Paris and the university cities, with close ties to Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva.

Inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood and Mawdudi's Jamaat-e-Islami, the association teaches Islam as a complete way of life, holds study circles and lectures and publishes pamphlets in French. It rejects secular nationalism, Marxism and Western materialism, but prefers education and preaching to political action. Its leverage lies in training an educated elite that will carry the Islamic revival home or settle in France.

13.name: L'Énarchie
13.text:
The Enarchy is the mocking name given in 1967 by Jean-Pierre Chevènement and fellow young civil servants, writing as Jacques Mandrin, to the caste of graduates of the National School of Administration founded by Michel Debré in 1945. Énarques fill the grands corps, the ministerial cabinets and the boards of state enterprises: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing runs Finance, Jacques Chirac the budget, and Simon Nora inspires Chaban-Delmas's reforms.

The technocrats believe France must be run by competent experts above party quarrels. They favour indicative planning, national champions in steel, aerospace, computers and nuclear power, and a state that guides capital rather than serving it. They are loyal to national independence but indifferent to ideology. Their leverage lies in drafting every budget, decree and plan.

14.name: Centre démocrate
14.text:
The Democratic Centre was founded in 1966 by Jean Lecanuet, who had won 15 per cent against de Gaulle in the presidential election of 1965, to unite the Christian democrats of the former Popular Republican Movement with moderate conservatives. Its standard-bearer Alain Poher, President of the Senate, stood in for de Gaulle as interim President in 1969 and won 42 per cent against Pompidou, but Jacques Duhamel's centrists have since defected to the government.

The Centre stands for Christian social values, a federal united Europe, the Atlantic Alliance, decentralisation and a more parliamentary republic, and it opposes Gaullist personal power. Its strongholds are the Catholic west, Alsace, Lorraine and the Senate, and its leverage lies in the arithmetic of a divided majority.

15.name: Conseil national du patronat français
15.text:
The National Council of French Employers was founded in 1946 to speak for French business, uniting federations from steel, chemicals and cars to banking and retail. Its president Paul Huvelin and its vice-president for social affairs François Ceyrac are still digesting the wage rises conceded at Grenelle in May 1968, while Chaban-Delmas presses for contractual policies and 'progress contracts' in the public sector.

The CNPF defends free enterprise, managerial authority and the market against nationalisation and union power. It accepts planning and European integration as long as they serve competitiveness, and supports mergers into large groups able to face American and German rivals. Its leverage lies in investment, prices, the banks and the access of France's great industrial families to ministers.

16.name: Parti républicain, radical et radical-socialiste
16.text:
The Radical Party, founded in 1901, is the oldest party in France and was once the pivot of the Third Republic, but it has dwindled to a network of provincial notables, especially in the south-west. In October 1969 the press magnate Jean-Jacques Servan-Schreiber, founder of L'Express and author of 'The American Challenge', became its secretary-general under the presidency of Maurice Faure, promising to rebuild it as a modern reform party.

The Radicals defend free enterprise, small business, secular schools, regional power and a federal Europe, and want to separate economic power from inherited ownership. They oppose Gaullist centralism and the Communists alike. Their base is shopkeepers, farmers, teachers and Freemasons in small towns, and their leverage lies in Senate seats, local councils and Servan-Schreiber's media flair.

17.name: Fédération française des sociétés de protection de la nature
17.english: French Federation of Nature Protection Societies
17.native_full: Fédération française des sociétés de protection de la nature
17.text:
The French Federation of Nature Protection Societies was founded in 1968 to unite naturalist clubs, regional conservation societies and the venerable National Society for the Protection of Nature. Its cause has been sharpened by the ornithologist Jean Dorst's warning book 'Before Nature Dies' and by the battle against a ski resort project inside the Vanoise National Park, as the Council of Europe proclaims 1970 European Conservation Year.

The Federation stands for national parks and nature reserves, protection of birds and wetlands, limits on pesticides and resistance to concrete on coasts and mountains. It is non-party and moderate, relying on scientists, teachers and local associations, though younger activists are beginning to speak of ecology as politics. Its leverage lies in expertise, petitions and public opinion.

18.name: Parti socialiste unifié
18.text:
The Unified Socialist Party was founded in 1960 by left socialists, dissident radicals and left-wing Catholics who opposed the Algerian war and the compromises of the old SFIO. Its national secretary Michel Rocard won 3.6 per cent in the 1969 presidential election and in October defeated the former Prime Minister Maurice Couve de Murville in a by-election in the Yvelines.

The PSU preaches workers' self-management, decentralisation and a socialism free of both Soviet bureaucracy and social-democratic compromise. It backs the Third World and Vietnam, opposes NATO and the nuclear strike force, and embraced the spirit of May 1968. Its base is students, teachers, engineers, activists of the CFDT union and progressive Catholics, and its leverage lies in ideas that are reshaping the whole left.

19.name: Gauche prolétarienne
19.text:
The Proletarian Left was founded in the autumn of 1968 by Maoist militants from the Union of Communist Youth (Marxist-Leninist) and the March 22 Movement. Its secret leader is the normalien Benny Lévy, known as Pierre Victor, with Alain Geismar and Serge July among its public faces; its newspaper La Cause du peuple calls openly for revolt, and its militants have taken factory jobs to radicalise workers.

The GP believes France is ripe for a popular uprising and a 'new Resistance' against bosses, police and the Gaullist state. It reveres Mao's China, despises the PCF as revisionist and practises spectacular direct action, from factory sequestrations to street fights. Its base lies in elite universities, lycées and among some immigrant and young workers, and its leverage in daring and publicity.

20.name: Comité d'information et de défense
20.text:
The Committee of Information and Defence was founded in 1969 by Gérard Nicoud, a young café owner from La Bâtie-Montgascon in the Isère, to defend small shopkeepers, artisans and independent workers against taxes, social charges and the spread of supermarkets. Its blockades, tax strikes and raids on tax offices have revived the spirit of Pierre Poujade's revolt of the 1950s, and it is drawing closer to the National Union of Independent Workers.

The movement speaks for the little man crushed between big business and the fiscal state. It demands tax justice, pensions for the self-employed and limits on hypermarkets, and denounces technocrats, Parisian elites and modernisation imposed from above. Its leverage lies in direct action, the anger of provincial town centres and the votes of the self-employed.

20.name: Front national
20.text:
The National Front was founded on 5 October 1972 on the initiative of the neo-fascist movement New Order, which wanted a respectable electoral front for the legislative elections of 1973. Its president is Jean-Marie Le Pen, a former Poujadist deputy, paratroop officer in Algeria and organiser of Jean-Louis Tixier-Vignancour's presidential campaign of 1965, with the journalist François Brigneau among its leaders.

The Front unites nationalists, Algérie française veterans, Poujadists, Catholic traditionalists and neo-fascists against the Gaullist 'regime' and the Union of the Left. It calls for order, anti-communism, the defence of small business and the family, and an end to uncontrolled immigration. Its votes are few, but its leverage lies in uniting the scattered far right behind one name.

21.name: Ordre nouveau
21.text:
New Order was founded on 15 December 1969 by veterans of the neo-fascist group Occident, dissolved by the government in 1968, and other activists of the nationalist far right. Its president is the lawyer Jean-François Galvaire, while former Occident militants such as Alain Robert and the historian François Duprat shape its line, and allied student shock troops dominate the law faculty in the rue d'Assas.

New Order preaches revolutionary nationalism, anti-communism and the solidarity of European nationalists, taking inspiration from the Italian Social Movement. It despises Gaullism and parliamentary democracy, glorifies street combat with the leftists under the Celtic cross and dreams of a disciplined, hierarchical nation. Its leverage is limited to violence, provocation and the small but determined networks of the French far right.

22.name: Forces armées françaises
22.text:
The French Armed Forces have rebuilt themselves since the trauma of Algeria, the failed generals' putsch of 1961 and the purge of the officer corps that followed; the last convicted officers were amnestied in 1968. The Chief of the Defence Staff, General Michel Fourquet, serves under the Minister of National Defence Michel Debré, and French troops are fighting rebels in Chad at the request of President Tombalbaye.

The army is now a disciplined instrument of national independence: it guards the nuclear strike force of Mirage IV bombers and the coming missile submarines and silos, keeps garrisons in Germany and Africa and relies on conscription. Officers remain conservative and anti-communist but loyal to the Republic. Their leverage lies in the deterrent and France's African commitments.

23.name: Maison d'Orléans
23.text:
The House of Orléans, a cadet branch of the Bourbons, is represented by Henri, Count of Paris, pretender to the throne of France since 1940. Having broken with the Action française in the 1930s, he cultivated de Gaulle, who for a time seemed to consider him a possible successor; the General's fall in April 1969 has ended that hope. A legitimist minority backs the Spanish Bourbons, while the Restauration nationale keeps Maurras's royalist doctrine alive.

The Count of Paris presents himself as a modern, social and democratic monarch above parties, attentive to workers and to national unity. Royalism is marginal, but it survives among Catholic aristocrats, traditionalist intellectuals and readers of Aspects de la France. Its leverage is the prestige of the dynasty that made France.
